title: Opinion: Chalmers' tax on unrealised super gains is clever, and cruel to the unadvised
summary: A critical view of the proposed tax on high-balance super that shows how a tax on unrealised gains can fall on people who do not expect to be caught, which is useful for evaluating equity and efficiency.
lede: AFR wealth reporter Andrew Hobbs argues the proposed tax on unrealised gains in super balances above $3 million will initially hit hardly anyone, but will catch unsophisticated investors holding illiquid assets as property values rise. The government says fewer than 80,000 people (0.5 per cent of account holders) are affected, a figure the article notes dates from February 2023.

figures.label: Super balance threshold for the proposed tax
Share of super account holders affected at start
Share of account holders paying by 2053
Super contribution rate used in author's example

terms.def: An increase in the value of an asset that has not yet been sold, so no cash has been received.
A threshold that is not adjusted for inflation, so more people reach it over time.
Those with a greater capacity to pay contribute more tax.

angle: Use as the opposing view when you evaluate the equity of taxing high-balance super: the policy is progressive in intent but the article argues it is poorly targeted at the unadvised.

questions.q: Explain why a tax on unrealised gains may be seen as less fair than a tax on realised gains.
Outline why not indexing the $3 million threshold matters over time.

note: Older item (published May 2025): figures are as at that date; check for newer data before quoting. Opinion piece, not a news report; the proposal was a draft and design details may differ from what was legislated. Newspaper article reproduced for classroom use. A second copy of the same article in the folder was skipped as a duplicate.

title: Australian economy data dashboard for Year 11, September 2026
summary: A single set of ten current indicators, each with its previous value and an exam hook, ready to quote with direction and source in any short answer or extended response.
lede: The dashboard collects the latest official figures at 2 September 2026: GDP growth of 0.4 per cent in the June quarter, headline inflation of 3.5 per cent, unemployment of 4.5 per cent and a cash rate of 4.35 per cent after three rises in 2026. It links them into a loop of prices, the RBA, borrowing and output, jobs and the federal Budget.

terms.def: Underlying inflation that removes the 15% of items with the largest price rises and the 15% with the largest falls.
Unemployment plus underemployment as a share of the labour force.
Whether the Budget is expansionary, contractionary or neutral, judged by the change in the balance as a share of GDP.
How a change in the cash rate reaches spending and prices.

angle: Quote direction as well as level (for example unemployment 4.5%, up from 4.4%) and link two indicators in each paragraph.

questions.q: Distinguish between headline and underlying inflation, using the 3.5% and 3.6% figures.
Explain how the three cash-rate rises in 2026 are expected to slow aggregate demand.
Assess whether a deficit of 1.0% of GDP is an appropriate fiscal stance when growth is below trend.

note: Teacher revision handout for Year 11 compiling official releases as at 2 September 2026; figures are as at that date and later releases will have updated them, so check the ABS and RBA before quoting. Budget figures for 2025-26 onwards are estimates, not outcomes.

title: Petrol thefts and petrol prices: a BOCSAR study turned into an elasticity lesson
outlets: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR)
summary: A real NSW dataset that applies price elasticity of demand, the total outlay method and supply shocks in the petrol market, and shows that cost of living matters more than price for theft.
lede: BOCSAR Bulletin No. 280 (August 2026) finds a 1 per cent rise in petrol prices raises petrol thefts by about 3 per cent over several months, around 37 extra incidents a month in NSW. The bigger driver is the general cost of living, with wages moving theft in the opposite direction.

figures.label: Increase in petrol thefts after a 1% rise in petrol prices
Extra petrol thefts a month across NSW
Average petrol thefts a month in NSW
Elasticity of theft with respect to wages
Elasticity of theft with respect to living costs
Elasticity of theft with respect to petrol prices

terms.def: Responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price: %change in quantity demanded divided by %change in price.
Judging elasticity from whether total spending (price times quantity) rises or falls when price changes.
A sudden change in the cost or availability of an input that shifts the supply curve.
Two series can move together because a third factor drives both.

angle: Use as a Year 11 stimulus for PED: inelastic demand means a supply shock lands on household budgets, which links to cost of living.

questions.q: Explain why the demand for petrol is price inelastic.
Using the worked example, apply the total outlay method to show demand is inelastic.
With reference to the stimulus, explain what the findings show about the importance of income compared with price.

note: Year 11 teacher summary of a BOCSAR bulletin: the document gives August 2026 but no day, so the date is set to the first of the month. Figure B and the worked example (180c to 198c, 500m to 485m litres) are hypothetical teaching figures, not results from the bulletin. Check the original bulletin before quoting.

title: Australia's income and wealth distribution infographic (McCrindle, 2023)
summary: A one-page picture of how unequally income and wealth are shared across household quintiles, states and generations, with ready-made ratios to quote.
lede: The top 20 per cent of households earn 48 per cent of all income and own 63 per cent of private wealth, while the lowest 20 per cent earn 4 per cent of income and own 1 per cent of wealth. The average household in the top quintile holds 93 times the wealth of the bottom quintile, and a median house costs 10.3 times average full-time earnings.

figures.label: Share of all income earned by the top 20% of households
Share of private wealth owned by the top 20% of households

terms.def: One fifth of households ranked by income.
The value of assets minus debts.
Income is a flow received over a period; wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time.

angle: Pair the income and wealth quintile shares to show that wealth inequality is wider, then use the generational table for age differences.

questions.q: Using the infographic, compare the distribution of income with the distribution of wealth.
Explain one reason wealth is more unequally distributed than income.

note: Older item (published 2023): figures are as at that date; check for newer data before quoting. Only the year (2023) is given, so the date is set to 1 January. Infographic from a social research company drawing on ABS and Domain data; secondary source.

title: Senate inquiry final report: The extent and nature of poverty in Australia
summary: The most authoritative recent source on Australian poverty rates, groups at risk and the role of income support, with 14 recommendations to cite in policy evaluation.
lede: The Senate committee's final report (February 2024) uses ACOSS and UNSW analysis to show 13.4 per cent of people, and 16.6 per cent of children, live below the poverty line after housing costs. It examines income support adequacy, employment services, First Nations poverty and child poverty and recommends urgent action to ensure no one lives in poverty.

Explain how income support payments can reduce poverty.

title: Treasury working paper: Estimating the NAIRU in Australia
summary: Treasury's own estimate that unemployment consistent with stable inflation is about 4.75 per cent, which defines how much spare capacity exists in the labour market.
lede: The Treasury working paper (April 2021) re-estimates the NAIRU using a wage Phillips curve and finds it lay between 4.5 and 5 per cent in the years before the COVID-19 recession, with a point estimate of 4.75 per cent. It warns the NAIRU cannot be observed and estimates carry large confidence intervals.

terms.def: The non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment: the rate consistent with stable wage growth and inflation.
The relationship between inflation (or wage growth) and unemployment.
The medium to long-run rate reflecting frictional and structural unemployment.

angle: Use the 4.75 per cent estimate with the caveat that it is unobservable: when unemployment sits below it, wage and price pressure tend to rise.

questions.q: Outline what is meant by the NAIRU.
Explain why the NAIRU is difficult to measure and what that means for policy.

title: Australia's population map and generational profile (McCrindle, 2023)
summary: A snapshot of Australia's demographics (population, age, cities, workforce) that supports answers on ageing, participation and the size of the labour force.
lede: Australia's population is 26.3 million with a median age of 38, and Sydney and Melbourne are each above 5 million. The infographic also shows labour market figures (14 million employed, 3.5 per cent unemployment) and how each generation's share of the workforce is projected to change by 2033.

title: Division 296 super tax as a microeconomic reform case study
summary: A ready-made case study applying the five economic objectives to a targeted tax reform on very large super balances.
lede: Division 296 applies an extra tax on earnings from super balances above $3 million, so earnings on that portion are taxed at 30 per cent instead of 15 per cent. The notes estimate it affects around 80,000 people (0.5 per cent of holders) and raises about $2.3 billion over four years, then assess its effects on growth, distribution, employment, price stability and the environment.

terms.def: A tax on the earnings attributable to the part of a super balance above $3 million.
The principle that those with greater ability to pay should pay more tax.
Changes that alter incentives and the operation of markets to improve efficiency and equity.

angle: Use the five-objective structure to build an evaluation paragraph on a targeted reform, noting the equity benefit and the limited revenue.

questions.q: Explain how a higher tax on earnings of very large super balances may affect the distribution of income and wealth.
Evaluate Division 296 as an example of microeconomic reform.

Teacher study notes, not an official source: the dollar figures are quoted from Treasury, Grattan, ABS and APRA as the notes cite them, and the policy details are as at mid-2025 and may have changed, so check the current legislated design before quoting.

title: Ken Henry's warning on tax reform, fairness and growth (student article)
summary: A long-form article on Australia's tax system that ties together incentives, intergenerational equity, housing, resource rents and carbon pricing for evaluation of tax policy.
lede: The article summarises a May 2026 speech by Dr Ken Henry arguing the tax system is 'more obviously broken' than at the time of the Henry Review, with too much reliance on personal income tax and favoured treatment of capital gains and resource rents. It uses reform history from the 1985 Tax Summit, the GST and the carbon price to explain why sound economics often fails politically.

title: Reform aftershocks: how the 2026 federal Budget plans were rolled back
summary: A case study of a microeconomic reform package that was softened under pressure, useful for weighing equity, dynamic efficiency and political feasibility.
lede: The classroom zine traces changes to the 2026 Budget tax package: concessions for small business, start-ups and testamentary trusts cost just $475 million over four years against an $8.1 billion revenue target. It also covers NDIS savings, a $3.6 billion childcare wage-subsidy extension, migration, housing, energy prices and bank resilience.

terms.def: Improvement in productivity and innovation over time.
Policy changes that alter incentives and market operation to improve efficiency, productivity and competition.
A trust set up under a will; the zine notes genuine ones were exempted from the 30% minimum tax floor.

angle: Use the policy trade-off lens (equity, fiscal sustainability, dynamic efficiency) to evaluate any reform that is later softened.

questions.q: Explain how the CGT changes could affect incentives to invest in start-ups.
Evaluate the extent to which the 2026 Budget rollback improved the design of microeconomic reform.

note: Classroom zine paraphrasing an AFR source pack and official Budget material; secondary source, check the Budget papers before quoting figures. No date in the document, so the file's modified date (19 Jun 2026) is used. Some policy details (for example the CGT start date) are as described in the zine.

title: RBA speech: monetary policy implementation and the move to ample reserves
summary: An RBA explanation of how the cash rate target is actually implemented through banks' reserves, which sits behind every 'RBA lowers the cash rate' headline.
lede: Assistant Governor Christopher Kent announced on 2 April 2025 that from 9 April the RBA would raise the price of new open market operation repos to 10 basis points above the cash rate target and add a seven-day term. He stressed these are operational changes, not a shift in the stance of monetary policy.

title: RBA's new framework for additional monetary policy tools: illustrated explainer
summary: A summary of how the RBA now plans to use unconventional monetary policy, including its own verdict on the pandemic-era tools, to evaluate effectiveness and limitations.
lede: Based on a 29 June 2026 speech and Q&A by Assistant Governor Christopher Kent, the explainer sets out four principles the RBA will apply before using additional tools and grades each of six tools. The pandemic term funding facility cost the RBA about $9 billion and bond purchases about $30 billion to date.

title: Treasurer's 2025-26 Budget Speech
summary: The government's own account of the 2025-26 Budget, showing its forecasts, its fiscal stance and the cost-of-living package in the Treasurer's words.
lede: Treasurer Jim Chalmers told Parliament on 25 March 2025 that inflation is down, unemployment is low and growth is picking up, with a $42 billion deficit forecast for 2025-26. The Budget includes $17 billion of new tax cuts, $1.8 billion more energy bill relief and a $33 billion plan to build 1.2 million homes.

terms.def: Whether the Budget is expansionary, contractionary or neutral.
Bringing inflation down without a sharp rise in unemployment.
Budget measures that reduce household costs, such as tax cuts and energy rebates.

angle: Compare the government's framing with an independent analysis such as the Deloitte report.

questions.q: Outline one way the 2025-26 Budget supports household incomes.
Explain what a deficit of $42 billion suggests about the fiscal stance.

note: Older item (published Mar 2025): figures are as at that date; check for newer data before quoting. Primary source from the Treasurer's website, but a political speech: figures are forecasts, and later Budgets have revised them.

title: Federal Budget 2025-26: A platform for the next election (Deloitte)
summary: An independent professional analysis that gives the Budget deficits and debt in more than one measure, useful for a critical view of fiscal sustainability.
lede: Deloitte says the underlying cash deficit is forecast at $27.6 billion (1.0 per cent of GDP) in 2024-25 but off-budget spending takes the headline deficit to $46.7 billion (1.7 per cent). It argues government spending has become the driver of growth and the medium-term outlook is getting worse, with net debt rising to 23.1 per cent of GDP in 2028-29.

figures.label: Headline cash deficit including off-budget spending

terms.def: Receipts minus payments, excluding one-off items.
Spending that is not counted in the headline Budget deficit.
The deficit that remains when the economy is at its normal level of activity.

angle: Use to show that headline deficits can hide off-budget spending, then assess sustainability using the debt projections.

questions.q: Explain why the underlying cash deficit may understate the true fiscal position.
Assess the sustainability of the government's fiscal position using the data in the report.

note: Older item (published Mar 2025): figures are as at that date; check for newer data before quoting. Analysis by a private firm, and the document includes opinion; forecasts have been revised by later Budget updates.
